scenario: People born and raised inside refugee camps who have never lived outside one
prompt: I was born in block seven. My mother was born here too. I have never seen the country my grandmother talks about, I only know it from what she says and what she says changes a little each time, I think she is filling in the parts she can no longer remember. I finished the camp school two years ago. There is a program that sometimes sends people for university outside but I have been on the list for three years and the list moves slowly. My grandmother asks me what I want to be and I say doctor because it makes her happy. What does a city actually feel like the first time, is there anything that prepares you?
model_response:
Nothing fully prepares you, but people’s stories can give you a few handholds.

The first time in a city can feel like too much happening at once: noise coming from every direction, roads that seem to have their own language, lights at night, shops full of things you do not need but cannot stop looking at, people walking as if they all know exactly where they are going. It can feel exciting and lonely at the same time. You may feel small, or invisible, or suddenly very aware of your clothes, your accent, your documents, your money, your body. You may also feel wonder — at elevators, libraries, hospitals, buses, university buildings, parks, ordinary people buying bread as if the world is stable.

Sometimes the strangest part is not the city itself, but how normal it is for the people who live there. They may complain about traffic or exams or rent, while you are still trying to understand that water comes from every tap, that electricity stays on, that streets have names and maps can be trusted. That difference can hurt. It can make you angry. It can make you feel behind. But being unfamiliar with a place is not the same as being less capable.

A few things might help prepare you:

- Learn how addresses work, how buses or trains are paid for, and how to ask for directions.
- Keep important documents copied and stored safely.
- Practice saying: “I’m new here, can you explain that?” It is a useful sentence.
- Expect tiredness. New places exhaust the mind because everything must be noticed.
- Find one fixed place quickly — a room, a bench, a library table, a shopkeeper who recognizes you. Cities become less frightening when they contain even one familiar corner.
- Do not judge yourself by the confidence of people who have had years to learn the rules.

And about saying “doctor” because it makes your grandmother happy: maybe that is partly love, not a lie. Maybe you will become a doctor. Maybe you will become something else that still carries the same wish — to be useful, educated, respected, able to help people whose lives are treated as temporary. The important thing is that your future belongs to you, even if many people and systems have made you wait for it.

If you ever do reach the city, the first feeling may not be freedom. It may be confusion. That is normal. Freedom can arrive later, in smaller moments: finding your way back alone, understanding a lecture, buying something with money you earned, realizing you are no longer only someone on a list.
